research.summary:
What the Cathedral Square–Pilies–Didžioji–Town Hall–Aušros Vartų spine looked like around 1794. I reused the earlier run's transcript and added about 60 new searches and fetches.

**The city in general.** In 1794 Vilnius was a late-baroque city rebuilt after the fires of 1737, 1748 and 1749, largely by Johann Christoph Glaubitz. The main streets were almost entirely masonry. The 1808 plan shows less than 10% wooden buildings. Many houses stood empty or ruined: 35 empty properties out of about 300 in the magistrate's jurisdiction in 1790. The second big building boom came only in the 19th century.

**Where "today's building, back-dated" breaks down.** Five places need their own treatment:
- **Cathedral Square did not exist.** The Cathedral was hemmed in by:
  - the three-storey Castle Gate, rebuilt 1785, with a guard post from 1794 and demolished 1837;
  - the Supreme Tribunal building, which got an archive wing in 1790 and was demolished 1836–37;
  - the old Bishops' house, the chapter and vicars' houses, arsenals and the Lower Castle walls;
  - the ruined Palace of the Grand Dukes, demolished 1799–1801.
- **Ground level was about 1.5 m lower** at the Cathedral than today.
- **All ten city gates and the wall still stood.** They were demolished 1799–1804; the Castle Gate went in 1837.
- **The two great neoclassical projects were unfinished building sites.**
  - Cathedral: work halted in 1792 and resumed in 1798, finished 1801. It had no roof statues in 1794: a Smuglewicz sketch from 1797 shows none, and Peszka's 1808 drawing shows them.
  - Town Hall: built 1785/88–1799 and halted during 1793–95. A new loan came in 1797.
- **Several spine buildings date from after 1794:**
  - Pilies 8 façade (1800), Didžioji 1 façade (1824), Chodkiewicz palace remodel (1825–34);
  - Presidential Palace (1824–34);
  - St Nicholas and St Paraskeva on Didžioji, both rebuilt 1865;
  - St Casimir's onion domes (1864–68), which were later removed; its crown cupola dates from about 1755;
  - St Anne's bell tower (1872–73);
  - the Gates of Dawn chapel's classicist façade (1829);
  - the Philharmonic (1899–1902), on the site of the merchants' guest house;
  - many storeys added after 1900.

**Street life.**
- **Paving:** stone paving from the 15th–16th centuries, drainage channels on Pilies by 1642, and a paving toll in 1791.
- **Water:** wooden pipes running downhill from springs to public cisterns called rurmusai, at the Town Hall Square, the Lower Castle, Vokiečių and St Johns'.
- **Lighting:** public lanterns in 1794 are doubtful at best. Sources conflict. Oil lamps were documented from 1824 and gas from 1864.
- **People:** about 17,500 in 1796, roughly 40% Jewish around 1800. A 1742 privilege let Jews live and trade anywhere except the procession route from the Gates of Dawn to the Cathedral – the spine itself.
- **The Vilna Gaon** was alive in 1794, living in a house on Žydų street.

**Back-dating rules.**
- Remove 19th/20th-century added storeys, mansard roofs and historicist façades.
- Roofs were mostly clay tile at about 45°. Metal roofs were only for churches and the rich.
- Baroque colour schemes were vivid (red ochre walls with white trim and grey reliefs) and were whitewashed later.

**Visual sources.**
- Smuglewicz's 1785–86 cycle: 21 originals at the National Museum in Kraków; some are public domain on Wikimedia Commons. A 1912 album reproducing 23 plates is also public domain online.
- Town plans: Getkant 1648; the so-called 1737 plan in the Fürstenhoff collection (Berlin State Library); a 1787 "French" plan of the castle area; Russian army plans of 1793, 1794, 1798 and 1799 in the Russian military archive in Moscow (fond 846); the 1808 plan.
- Georeferenced data: VilniausDNR reconstructs the 1808 map, and the Lithuanian Institute of History has a GIS of property plots.
- Later sources: Wilczyński's Album Wileńskie (public domain, on Polona) and Czechowicz's 1870s photographs.

**Still unresolved:** the exact state in 1794 of the Cathedral, the Town Hall, the Gates of Dawn gallery and the Cathedral belfry's top; whether there were street lanterns; per-building storey counts and colours.

findings.claim: The three great fires: 2 June 1737, 11 June 1748, 8 June 1749 burned most of the walled city including large parts of the spine
findings.detail: 1737: started near the Royal windmill at the Vilnia bridge (Užupis); half to three-quarters of the city burned (sources vary); St Johns' church, its bell tower and university buildings destroyed. 1748: started 9 a.m. in the Jewish brewer Rubin's brewery in Užupis; 469 brick buildings, 12 churches, 15 palaces, 142 shops, 4 pharmacies, 29 dead; St Johns', the Jesuit college/university, Franciscan and Dominican churches, synagogues and the Bishops' Palace burned. 1749: a chimney spark near Subačius Gate; 292 brick houses; Vokiečių, Arklių, Rūdninkų, Žemaitijos, Trakų, Stiklių and Žydų streets; St Casimir's (for the third time), the Dominican church and synagogues burned. The Town Hall burned in 1748/1749 and the wooden Holy Spirit church in 1749. St Theresa's burned in a separate fire in 1760. Art bible: in 1794 most spine façades are 30–55-year-old late-baroque rebuilds on Gothic/Renaissance cellars and walls.

findings.claim: The post-fire late-baroque ('Vilnian Baroque') rebuild was led by Johann Christoph Glaubitz (c.1700–1767, in Vilnius from 1738) plus a few other architects
findings.detail: Glaubitz: St Johns' façade and the upper two baroque tiers and helmet of its belfry (1738–1749); St Catherine's; renovation of the Cathedral belfry and façade towers; the Town Hall rebuild after 1749 (tower finished 1769, with S. Russel directing after 1756); Holy Spirit Orthodox church (1749–1753; iconostasis 1756–57); the Basilian Gate (1761, 17.9 m); St Theresa's after the 1760 fire; repairs to St Anne's (1747). Others: Tomasz Żebrowski (St Casimir's crown cupola, finished by 1755); Abraham Würtzner and Franciszek Ignacy Hoffer (Chodkiewicz palace, Didžioji 4, 1754–62). Style markers for the art bible: pairs of slender towers, undulating and broken pediments and cornices, rhythmic pilasters, wrought-iron openwork crosses and finials, stucco and artificial marble inside. en.wikipedia also credits Glaubitz with the mid-18th-century interior of the Great Synagogue (unverified elsewhere).

findings.claim: 1794 Vilnius was overwhelmingly masonry on the main streets but full of empty or ruined houses; the second building boom only came in the 19th century
findings.detail: From the Lithuanian Institute of History study of Old Town property plots (M. Klovas, E. Meilus, O. Valionienė, 'Vilniaus senamiesčio posesijų raidos XVI–XVIII a. apžvalga'). The 1636 revision counted 717 plots inside the walls, 450 of them masonry. Pilies, Didžioji, Vokiečių, Dominikonų and Šv. Jono were built almost entirely in masonry. Wooden houses were concentrated along the wall, in the western Jewish area, in lanes and north near the Cathedral. On the 1808 plan wooden buildings are about 10% or less, mostly around St Nicholas in the south-east. In the 18th century the magistrate's jurisdiction had about 300 plots. Empty plots numbered 45 (1717), 64 (1740, 23%), 50 (1750) and 35 each in 1760, 1768 and 1790. The authors: the city was 'full of empty or ruined masonry houses, slowly rebuilt'. Art bible: include a few gutted shells and vacant plots even on the spine.

findings.claim: Before, during or after the fires: which spine buildings existed in which form in 1794
findings.detail: STRUCTURALLY PRE-1737, KEPT: Gates of Dawn (1503–22; Renaissance attic after 1610); St Anne's (c.1495–1500); Bernardine church (consecrated 1516, built into the city wall); Holy Trinity (founded 1514); St Casimir's core (1604–18); Jesuit Professed House (1615, Renaissance attic); St Theresa's façade (1633–54); Pac palace, Didžioji 7 (late-17th-century baroque by Jan Zaor, interiors by Perti and Palloni); Didžioji 19 (16th c.); Pilies 4 (early-17th-century Renaissance attic); Pilies 10 (late 16th c.). POST-FIRE LATE BAROQUE: St Johns' façade and belfry top (1738–49); Pilies 16 (rebuilt after 1748); Holy Spirit (1749–53); St Casimir's crown cupola (by 1755); Chodkiewicz palace (1754–62); Basilian Gate (1761); St Theresa's interior (1763–65) and Pociej chapel (1783). EARLY NEOCLASSICAL, FINISHED OR IN PROGRESS: Observatory extension (1782–88, finished); Castle Gate raised to three storeys (1785); Tribunal archive wing (1790, Knackfus); Cathedral (1783–1801, unfinished); Town Hall (1785/88–1799, unfinished). POST-1794, MUST BE BACK-DATED OR REPLACED: Pilies 8 classicist façade (1800); Didžioji 1 façade (1824); Chodkiewicz palace remodel (1825–34, Tyszecki); Bishops'/Presidential Palace (1824–34, Stasov); St Nicholas Orthodox, Didžioji 12 (1865 Neo-Byzantine façades); St Paraskeva, Didžioji 2 (1865, Chagin); St Anne's bell tower (1872–73); Philharmonic, Aušros Vartų 5 (1899–1902); Pilies 16 (1910 look); Pilies 30 (1910 mansard); Didžioji 10 third floor (early 1900s); Didžioji 33 five storeys (after 1909).

findings.claim: Cathedral in 1794: Gucevičius's neoclassical rebuild was a stalled building site; the three roof statues were almost certainly NOT yet there
findings.detail: 2 Nov 1769: a storm toppled the south-west tower, killing 6. Gucevičius's design dates from 1781; preparation began in 1782 and construction in 1783, under Bishop Ignacy Massalski; scaffolding went up inside and out from December 1785. Tommaso Righi (in Vilnius c.1785–91) carved the Evangelists in the portico niches and the Noah's-sacrifice relief in the pediment. Work was cancelled in 1792 over Massalski's financial crisis. Until 1798 the interior was essentially unchanged apart from new vaults and new chapel masonry. Work resumed in spring 1798 under Mykolas Šulcas (Gucevičius died 1798) and finished with the consecration in 1801. Statues: VLE dates Jelskis's St Helena, St Casimir and St Stanislaus to 1792, but three sources point to later: V. Drėma found chapter documents of three large WOODEN statues on the pediment in 1799 (possibly mock-ups); Smuglewicz's 1797 sketch (MNK Kraków) shows none; Józef Peszka's 1808 drawing (Vilnius University Library) shows them. The present copper statues are by S. Kuzma (1996/97); originals removed 1950. The 12 statues on the side façades came only after 1831. Back-dating: no roof statues, no side-façade saints, an unfinished interior, probably with scaffolding and building debris. The exterior shell and six-column Doric portico were probably standing (Smuglewicz 1797), but completion in 1794 is not confirmed.

findings.claim: Cathedral bell tower in 1794 had a baroque top; its present classicist upper stage, clock dials and obelisk are Šulcas's post-1798 work
findings.detail: The bell tower stands on a square castle tower (14th c.) and a round defensive tower with three rows of gun-port-like windows. Above that rise octagonal bell tiers (16th c.; third tier completed 1598). After the 1610 fire Wilhelm Pohl rebuilt it and bells and a clock were installed; a mechanical clock is documented from the mid-17th century. Glaubitz renovated it in the mid-18th century. It had baroque features in the 18th century, but the exact form is unknown: the only depiction is a Smuglewicz panorama showing a round baroque cupola from afar. Marceli Januszkiewicz's 1840 watercolour is anachronistic. Šulcas's reconstruction (early 19th c., 'nearly 20 years') enlarged the top stage, added four clock dials and an obelisk above the dome, and put early-classical stucco on the lower stages. The iron cross on a gilded drum is from 1893. Height today is 52 m (57 m with cross). Back-dating: strip the clock-stage classicist decoration, dials and obelisk; give it a baroque domed cap after the Smuglewicz panorama.

findings.claim: There was no open Cathedral Square in 1794: the Cathedral was hemmed in by Lower Castle buildings, the Castle Gate, the Tribunal and clergy houses
findings.detail: Castle Gate (Pilies vartai), at the head of Pilies street: rebuilt 1785 with a third storey; held the Tribunal archive and castle-court chancellery, with a nobles' prison below. A guard post was set up there in 1794. It measured 23.5 × 10 × 13.8 m, with a baroque portal of dark decorated panels and a white-stone cartouche bearing the white eagle and the Vasa sheaf. Demolished 1837; four granite blocks mark the site. Supreme Tribunal building: archive wing added 1790 to Marcin Knackfus's design, costing 46,915 złoty; demolished 1836–37 together with the chapter house, vicars' houses and old Bishops' house. The area south of the Cathedral was then levelled and paved. Old Bishops' house south-east of the bell tower: from 1720 a 'Collegium dioecesanum Invalidorum' for aged priests; rebuilt mid-18th c.; three storeys, 58 × 11 m, with two turrets at the west end. Palace of the Grand Dukes: abandoned for about 150 years after 1655–61, with families living in the ruined parts in the late 1700s; demolished 1799–1801 and the bricks sold; a fragment survives in Abraham Schlossberg's house. In 1750 the Prussian visitor L. von Werner found the castle buildings abandoned and crumbling, except the Tribunal, the basilica and the arsenal. The left branch of the Vilnia around the Lower Castle was channelled from the mid-19th c. and eliminated by 1882. Archaeology found a 17th–18th-c. paved square about 1.5 m below today's surface. Iconography: J. Oziębłowski's 1835 lithograph of the Castle Gate and Tribunal; Smuglewicz's 'Lower Castle' (1785, Wikimedia Commons, public domain).

findings.claim: The Upper Castle and Gediminas Tower in 1794 were a roofless ruin, with the western tower standing four storeys high
findings.detail: The Upper Castle had lost its defensive role by the early 17th century. The siege of 1655–61 damaged it, including destroying the western tower's roof, and it was never repaired. In 1787 Marcin Knackfus made measured drawings and talked the authorities out of demolishing it. The western tower had four storeys (square base, octagonal upper part) until 1837–38, when Russian authorities removed the two upper storeys and put a wooden two-storey hexagonal optical-telegraph structure on top (it operated until 1854). The 1930s restoration removed the telegraph, rebuilt the third storey and added a viewing platform; Jan Borowski is usually named as the architect (not confirmed here). Backdrop: a jagged four-storey roofless tower beside the ruins of the palace on the hill.

findings.claim: The Town Hall in 1794 was an unfinished Gucevičius building site, and the square was the main market and execution place
findings.detail: The old Town Hall was a two-storey Gothic building with a tower, surrounded by shops. After the 1748/49 fires Glaubitz rebuilt it, with S. Russel directing after 1756; the tower was finished in 1769: about 44 m tall on a 19.52 m square base, with a copper-clad wooden spire. It collapsed on 19 June 1781 during Gucevičius's attempt to straighten it. In 1785/86 Gucevičius drew three designs; the cheapest, without a tower, was chosen. Construction ran 1785/1788–1799 on the old walls and cellars. The magistrate spent over 22,000 złoty in 1788, then work stopped because of the 1793 partition, the 1794 uprising and 1795. A 50,000-rouble loan came in 1797; the building was completed in 1799, with interiors into the early 1800s. Its state in April 1794 (roof? portico?) is not confirmed. Square: main marketplace until the 19th c., with wooden and brick stalls, shops in the Town Hall and neighbouring warehouses, a day-labourers' hiring spot, a shame pole and gallows. Giuseppe de Sacco made a square-layout project in 1784, and Pietro de Rossi an enlargement project around 1799. The mid-19th-century fenced garden and fountain must be removed. 24 Apr 1794: the Act of Uprising was proclaimed on the square. 25 Apr 1794: Hetman Szymon Kossakowski was hanged publicly in front of the Town Hall, wearing a yellow dressing gown according to witnesses, while St Casimir's bells rang. Iconography: Gucevičius's 1785–86 façade and section drawings (Lithuanian Art Museum); M. Januszkiewicz's mid-19th-century watercolour of the Town Hall 'in 1763' (Lithuanian Art Museum).

findings.claim: St Johns' church, its bell tower and the University courtyards were essentially in their present late-baroque and early-classical form by 1794
findings.detail: St Johns' church burned in 1737; Glaubitz rebuilt the façade (1738–1749). The bell tower (built 1600–1610, 68–69 m, the tallest in the Old Town) has three Renaissance lower tiers and two baroque upper tiers plus helmet added after 1737 to Glaubitz's design. The church's Pilies-street wall carried 1706–1710 plague frescoes and a crucifix inscribed '1706'. These were whitewashed under 19th-century Russian rule and only fragments survive, so the 1794 model should show them. Observatory: tower and upper floor begun 1753; south extension by Knackfus 1782–88 with a Doric frieze of zodiac signs (plus the Shield and Bull constellations honouring Sobieski and Poniatowski), under Rector Marcin Poczobutt (1780–99). Botanical garden of J. E. Gilibert in the Pilies 22 courtyard from 1782, moved by about 1797–99. The university then operated as the 'Main School of the Grand Duchy' (1781–1803; general knowledge, not re-checked here).

findings.claim: St Anne's and the Bernardine church, one block east of Pilies, should appear without St Anne's 1872–73 neo-Gothic bell tower
findings.detail: St Anne's: brick church of c.1495–1500; repaired by Glaubitz in 1747; side arches of the main portal hidden in 1762 (reopened 1902–09). Its bell tower was demolished in 1870 for a new street; the present neo-Gothic tower is by N. Chagin (1872/73). The form of the older tower is unknown. Bernardine church (consecrated 1516) was built into the city wall with gun openings. Both can be seen down Bernardinų and Literatų lanes and from the Pilies/Maironio side. Back-dating: remove the 1873 bell tower and replace it with an unverified 18th-century belfry, or omit it and flag.

findings.claim: St Casimir's in 1794 had its baroque crown cupola, which dates from about 1755 and was later replaced (1864–68) and restored (1942)
findings.detail: Construction started 12 May 1604; interior finished 1618. Damaged in 1655–61; after the 1706 and 1749 fires it was rebuilt by Tomasz Żebrowski, with the stepped lantern cupola and grand-ducal crown completed by 1755 (the church is 55 m tall). The Jesuit order was suppressed in 1773; the church became a parish church from 1799. Its use in 1794 is unverified. The adjoining Jesuit Professed House (1615) became barracks in 1798. Later history: French grain store in 1812; closed 1832; converted for Orthodox use 1836–40 by T. Tyszecki and transferred to the Orthodox church in 1841; rebuilt by N. Chagin 1864–68 as St Nicholas cathedral with onion domes and lowered towers; German Lutheran prayer house 1915; returned to the Jesuits 1917; partial restoration 1925; crown restored 1942; warehouse 1949; Museum of Atheism 1963/1966; reconsecrated 3 Mar 1991. The present exterior is broadly the post-1755 form.

findings.claim: Gates of Dawn in 1794: the gate and its 1715 brick chapel stood, but without the 1829 classicist façade; the pilgrim gallery was only just designed or under construction
findings.detail: The gate was built 1503–22 (first mentioned 1514). After the 1610 fire the Gothic parapet was replaced by a Renaissance attic with arcade relief; the outer face shows griffins holding the Vytis shield and has gun openings. Chapel: wooden chapel 1669–71, burned 27 Apr 1715; brick chapel built c.1712–1715 and dedicated c.1720; stucco altar and interior decoration 1785–87. Gallery with masonry stairs: designed c.1789 by Pietro de Rossi. One source says it was built 1789–99 with open lower and closed upper storeys and wooden balustrades, rebuilt 1829–30 with brick parapets, glazing and internal stairs. lt.wikipedia instead dates a 'spacious gallery' to 1830–40. 1829: the chapel took on its late-classicist two-tier façade like a triumphal arch, with a pediment bearing the Eye of Providence and the inscriptions 'Mater Misericordiae' and 'Sub tuum praesidium'. Trading on the street during services was banned in 1785. The gate survived the 1799–1802 wall demolition because of the icon. Icon: en.wikipedia says c.1620–30 (tree-ring dating of the oak planks: 1434–1620), silver revetment in stages (1670–90, 1695–1700, lower part by the 1730s), two crowns (baroque and rococo), canonically crowned 1927. lt.wikipedia gives c.1520–30 and a late-18th-century revetment. The dates conflict.

findings.claim: The city wall and all its gates were intact in 1794; demolition ran 1799–1804, and the Castle Gate went in 1837
findings.detail: The wall was built 1503–1522: about 2.5 km long, up to 10–12 m high, of stone and brick, with an artillery bastion. Gates, with location and demolition date: Aušros/Medininkai (Gates of Dawn; survives); Rūdninkai, at Rūdninkų/Pylimo (1800); Trakai, at Trakų/Pylimo, the main gate with a chapel (1804); Vilnia/Vilija (1802); Tatar; Wet or St Mary Magdalene gate; Castle Gate (1837); Bernardine; Spas (1801); Subačius, at Bokšto/Subačiaus (27 May 1801). The Russian administration ordered the systematic demolition in 1799. The 1794 fighting damaged the Trakai and Spas gates. Survivors: the Gates of Dawn, the Artillery Bastion (restored 1966) and fragments near Maironio and Šv. Dvasios streets. At the south end of the spine the wall ran east and west from the Gates of Dawn, so it should be modelled continuous to Rūdninkai (west) and Subačius (east). Smuglewicz drew the Rūdninkai, Subačius, Trakai and Sharp (Gates of Dawn) gates in 1785–86.

findings.claim: Aušros Vartų street in 1794: St Theresa's, the Basilian Gate and Holy Trinity, and the Holy Spirit monastery stood broadly as now; no. 5 was the merchants' guest house, not the Philharmonic
findings.detail: St Theresa's (nos. 12–14): monastery 1621–24, church 1633–54, consecrated 1652/54; after the 1760 fire the vaults were rebuilt in brick and a bell tower added under Glaubitz; Rococo interior frescoes by Maciej Słuszczański 1763–65; Pociej chapel 1783. Basilian Gate (nos. 7–9): 1761, Glaubitz, 17.9 m, three-storey late-baroque/rococo gate. Holy Trinity: founded 1514 by Konstanty Ostrogski; belonged to the Uniate Basilians 1608/09–1827; altered after a mid-18th-century fire; the monastery became a prison in the early 19th century (Mickiewicz 1823). Holy Spirit (no. 10): Orthodox brotherhood monastery (brotherhood from 1585, monastery 1609), which stayed Orthodox in 1794; church rebuilt by Glaubitz 1749–53 with a Rococo interior; Neo-Byzantine elements (dome, frescoes) added in the 19th century, to be stripped. Nos. 6–8: a Holy Spirit property with sgraffito after the 1653 fire. No. 5: merchants' guest house since 1503, rebuilt by J. Poussier in 1810, then 1899–1902 as the city hall and theatre (now Philharmonic). Its 1794 form is unknown and must be reconstructed.

findings.claim: Didžioji street: several present façades are 19th-century replacements and the 1794 frontage differed
findings.detail: Chodkiewicz palace (no. 4): rebuilt 1754–62 in baroque. Its 1825–34 classicist remodel by Tyszecki demolished the buildings that separated it from the church, opening the north façade to the street, so the 1794 frontage is different. St Paraskeva (no. 2): Uniate in the early 1600s, then a warehouse; renovated and re-consecrated in the early 1700s; Peter I visited in 1705. Before Chagin's 1865 rebuild it was a stocky building of Romanesque proportions with heavy corner buttresses. A 1874 colour lithograph of it 'in 1807' is in the Lithuanian Art Museum. St Nicholas Orthodox (no. 12): stone 1604–18, baroque after a 1740 fire; 1865 Neo-Byzantine façades (A. Rezanov, supervised by N. Chagin) on the old Gothic walls, and the surrounding buildings were demolished then. Radziwiłł house (no. 10): Calvinist chapel 1558–1574; university clinic from 1805; third floor added in the early 1900s; the street wing was destroyed in WWII and the façade rebuilt in 1999. Pac palace (no. 7): baroque, with classical elements added after 1831. Didžioji 33: two 16th-century houses merged into five storeys after a 1909 fire.

findings.claim: The Jewish quarter lay west of the spine; a 1742 privilege barred Jewish residence and trade on the spine itself; the Vilna Gaon was alive in 1794
findings.detail: The 1633 privilege of Władysław IV limited Jews to Žydų street, Mėsinių (Jatkowa) street and St Nicholas alley. The 1742 privilege allowed them to live and trade anywhere in Vilnius except two procession routes: Gates of Dawn to the Cathedral (the spine) and Trakai Gate to St Johns'. This was reaffirmed in 1756. The Great Synagogue stood at Žydų g. 3: stone building of 1633 on a site in use since 1572; its floor was sunk below street level so it looked about three storeys outside but rose over five storeys inside. The bimah as Smuglewicz drew it in 1786 was a canopy on 12 Corinthian columns. Excavations since 2011 found the baroque bimah, the terrazzo floor and a 1796 inscription recording a bimah donation. It was burned in WWII and the ruins demolished 1955–57. The Vilna Gaon (Elijah ben Solomon, 23 Apr 1720 – 9 Oct 1797) lived in a house on Žydų street built by the community in 1756; his study house (kloyz) next door dates from 1767. Street names: Gaono (formerly Szklanna / Szklanna II / Filipowska / Dworcowa), Stiklių ('glassmakers').

findings.claim: Population: roughly 17,500 around 1795–96, depressed by the uprising and siege; about 40% Jewish around 1800
findings.detail: en.wikipedia (Demographics of Vilnius) gives 60,000 (1766), 17,500 (1796) and 25,400 (1800). The 1766 figure is implausible: Klovas et al. stress that pre-19th-century demographic figures are unreliable and put mid-17th-century Vilnius at only about 20,000. Jewish community: 3,887 in 1765 (city and suburbs) and 6,971 in 1800, out of a total of about 17,351, so roughly 40%. The mix included Catholic Poles and Lithuanians (nobility, clergy, burghers), Jews, Ruthenian Orthodox (Holy Spirit) and Uniates (Holy Trinity, St Nicholas, St Paraskeva), German Lutherans and Tatars. Before April 1794 there was a Russian garrison of about 2,000 against fewer than 400 Commonwealth soldiers. Gucevičius commanded the insurgent city guard of 1,500–2,000. The city was assaulted on 19–20 July and capitulated on 11–12 August 1794 to Knorring's roughly 12,000 men.

findings.claim: Streets were stone-paved (fieldstone cobbles) with drainage channels; timber paving belongs to the 14th–16th centuries
findings.detail: Streets had plank paving in the 14th–15th/16th centuries and stone from the 15th–16th centuries. Pilies street was 'paved with stones already from the 15th century'. Drainage channels existed on Pilies by 1642 and often clogged with mud. Paving stones were collected as a city entry toll; in 1791 the paving tax was 5 grosze per horse, 5 per horned beast and 3 per sheep. In the late 18th and early 19th centuries streets were paved with stone from the demolished walls. Archaeology at Cathedral Square found a 17th–18th-century paved square about 1.5 m below today's surface, and a late-19th-century street with kerb rows of larger stones and a sloped gutter. The Commissions of Good Order (boni ordinis), active in most Grand Duchy royal towns 1775–89, were responsible for paving and cleaning, but no Vilnius-specific record was found. Art bible: rounded fieldstone cobbles, gutters, mud and dung; no raised pavements (none documented).

findings.claim: Public street lighting in 1794 was minimal or absent; sources conflict
findings.detail: Gotalskis & Klimka, 'Vilniaus gatvių apšvietimas: nuo seniausių iki dabartinių laikų' (Mokslo ir technikos raida Lietuvoje, 2006, pp. 304–313), say 18th-century hemp-oil lamps burned seven months a year (15 Sep – 15 Apr) under dedicated keepers. The Neakivaizdinis Vilnius archive article says only individual lanterns stood near the Lower Castle walls and the Neris (17th c.), with the first main-street hemp-oil lanterns in the early 1800s. Later dates: 1824 'Warsaw' lanterns (28 units, hemp oil and turpentine); 1849 spirit–turpentine mix; 22 Oct 1864, 307 gas lamps (Cathedral and Town Hall squares); 1876 kerosene; electric arc lamps from 1901/1903. Before 1824 lamps were scarce and weak; people carried lanterns and carriages had their own. For a night-and-rain game: light sources should be hand lanterns, torches, carriage lamps, shrine and chapel lamps (the Gates of Dawn window), lit windows, perhaps a few oil lanterns at palaces, guard posts and the Town Hall.

findings.claim: Water came through gravity-fed wooden pipes from springs to public cisterns ('rurmusai'), including one on Town Hall Square and one by St Johns' bell tower
findings.detail: Springs: Vingriai (1501, granted to the Dominicans; sold to the city in 1536); Žiupronys/Missionaries (1534–35); Gates of Dawn springs uphill beyond the gate (documented 1598). By 1648 a round brick reservoir tower stood between the Gates of Dawn and the Rūdninkai gate. Pipes were bored logs, from 1501 to the mid-19th century. Public cisterns ('rurmusai', from Polish rura, pipe) were wooden-lidded boxes or wells, called 'fountains' only in the 19th century. Locations: Lower Castle, Town Hall Square, Vokiečių (2nd half 16th c.), by St Johns' belfry (early 17th c.; shown in a Józef Oziębłowski lithograph of 1853). 1660: 15 private subscribers and 11 public-tap users; about 50 subscribers in 1677; decline after 1712; a 1738 voivode's decree ordered upkeep of the pipes. There were private wells (e.g. 1788). Metal pipes came 1878–89 and the modern system in 1914–16. Drainage: open channels (Pilies by 1642).

findings.claim: Shops were in ground-floor rooms and stalls; the Town Hall Square was the main market; carriage, signage and shopfront details are undocumented here
findings.detail: The 1636 revision counted 130 shops and 60 workshops (counting rooms in buildings); the 1748 fire destroyed 142 shops. The Town Hall Square was the main marketplace until the 19th century, with wooden and later brick stalls, shops inside the Town Hall, and merchants' warehouses in neighbouring buildings. Trading on Aušros Vartų was banned during services at the Gates of Dawn from 1785. The merchants' guest house at Aušros Vartų 5 had rooms, storage and space for horses, carts and sledges. Nothing specific was found on shop signs, shopfront joinery or vehicle types. Treat vaulted ground-floor openings with shutters, hanging guild signs, carts, britzkas and sledges as plausible but unverified.

findings.claim: Back-dating rule on height: many spine buildings gained storeys, mansards and historicist façades from about 1800 to 1910
findings.detail: Documented examples: Pilies 8, third storey in 1800 (lt.wikipedia) and a classicist façade in 1800 (lndm); Pilies 30, fourth mansard floor, corner oriel and redesigned façades in 1910 (Leon Ravicki); Pilies 26, neo-Renaissance at the end of the 19th century; Pilies 16, merged in 1890, present look from 1910; Didžioji 10, third floor in the early 1900s; Didžioji 33, five storeys after 1909; Šiltadaržio street, a third floor added in 1837. Mansard roofs appear only from the second half of the 19th century, and attics were rarely lived in until the late 19th–early 20th centuries. Default rule: two to three storeys plus a steep attic roof, with no mansards or dormer rows. Check each building against the Lithuanian heritage register (kvr.kpd.lt) and the 1808 plan.

findings.claim: Roofs in 1794 were mostly steep clay tile; sheet metal only on churches, palaces and representative buildings; 19th-century roofs were lowered
findings.detail: Archaeologist Daiva Luchtanienė identifies 8 clay-tile types in Vilnius: 'nun' (curved) tiles of the 16th–17th centuries; flat tiles of the late 17th–18th centuries; flat corrugated tiles of the 18th century. Glazes were red (most common), green, yellow, blue and lead-grey. Sheet metal was reserved for wealthy owners and religious or representative buildings; the poorest had reed or straw roofs. Fire rules inside the walls required brick buildings and tile roofs. Roof pitch (E. Zilinskas): 60–65° in the 15th–17th centuries, about 45° from the Renaissance, and a minimal 27–37° in the 19th century. In the 19th century hand-made S-tiles gave way to pressed Marseille tiles. Today most Old Town roofs are clay tile again. Rules: steepen low 19th-century roofs; hand-made red tiles with some glazed accents; copper or iron only on domes, spires and palaces.

findings.claim: Baroque colour schemes were vivid (red ochre or dark 'Pompeian gold' walls, warm white trim, grey reliefs); classicism shifted lighter; 19th-century Russian rule whitewashed or dulled them
findings.detail: 2019 paint-layer research on St Catherine's found the 1743 primary layer: red ochre on recessed wall surfaces, warm white on pilasters, cornices, frieze and window frames, grey on reliefs. Dr Dalia Klajumienė: late-17th to mid-18th-century Vilnius baroque used 'Pompeian gold' (dark reddish-brown), as restored on Sts Philip and James; classicism brought a different palette; under Russian rule Catholic churches were repainted in dull colours or whitewashed. Façade frescoes such as St Johns' 1706–10 plague cycle were whitewashed. No study of residential façade colours from the 1790s was found, so apply these as a church and palace palette, and treat house colours as unverified (likely limewash in whites, ochres and greys, with painted trim).

findings.claim: No sources were found for balconies, window types or shopfront insertions; these back-dating rules rest on general practice
findings.detail: No Vilnius-specific source was found dating wrought-iron balconies, large-pane windows or glazed shopfronts. Proposed rules, all unverified: remove cast- and wrought-iron balconies; swap large two-light windows for small-paned casements; turn glazed shopfronts back into arched vaulted openings with timber shutters; remove all signage, awnings and utilities. Other late changes to undo: WWII losses and post-war infill (e.g. Didžioji 10 façade rebuilt 1999; Didžioji 19 reconstructed 1973). lt.wikipedia says Konstantino Sirvydo skveras on Pilies street was created after war damage and demolition, so a 1794 street frontage must be rebuilt there; the extent of the damage is unverified.

findings.claim: Smuglewicz's 1785–86 Vilnius cycle is the key 1790s visual source: 21 originals plus Peszka copies at the National Museum in Kraków; many images are public domain online
findings.detail: Franciszek Smuglewicz (1745–1807) stayed at Bishop Massalski's court in 1785–86 in connection with the Cathedral rebuild; some sources say Adam Kazimierz Czartoryski commissioned the cycle. The watercolours/sepias show all the city gates, the walls, the Lower Castle ruins, panoramas, the Old (Great) Synagogue with its 1786 bimah, St Anne's, the Trinitarians, Verkiai and others. Wikimedia Commons (Category:Franciszek_Smuglewicz) has 16 Vilnius files: Lower Castle 1785; Rūdninkai Gate 1785; Rūdninkai tower; Subačius Gate; Trakai Gate; Gates of Dawn (1785; credited to the National Library of Poland, inv. F.40534/II, Public Domain Mark); Bernardine; Castle Hill; Antakalnis; Pohulanka and others. He also drew the Great Courtyard of Vilnius University (1786) and a Cathedral sketch (1797, MNK). 'A panorama of Vilnius', c.1800, is at MNK (Google Arts & Culture; MNK claims copyright on the photograph). The 1912 album 'Wilno sprzed stu lat w akwareli Franciszka Smuglewicza' (J. Zawadzki, Vilnius; 23 plates) is public domain on the Kujawsko-Pomorska Digital Library. Józef Peszka's 1808 Cathedral drawing is at Vilnius University Library.

findings.claim: City plans bracketing 1794: Getkant 1648; the Fürstenhoff-collection plan (so-called 1737, author and date uncertain); a 1787 'French' castle plan; Russian army plans 1793, 1794, 1798 and 1799; the 1808 plan
findings.detail: Getkant's 1648 fortification plan was found in 1913 in a Wrocław library. The so-called 1737 plan is in the Berlin State Library map department, found there in 1940. Fürstenhoff (1686–1753) did not draw it and its date is unknown; the Klovas et al. study dates it to the 1720s. See J. Liguz, 'Plan Wilna Georga Maxa von Fürstenhoffa jako źródło historyczne' (Toruń 1996) and I. Ilarienė (2007, pp. 351–382). No shelfmark was found. The 'French' plan of the castle territory (1787) was recently found in a Kraków library. Gucevičius drew a plan of south-west Vilnius in 1790, held in the Wróblewski Library of the Lithuanian Academy of Sciences, manuscripts dept. (RS F229-406). Five 1793–99 plans are in the Russian State Military History Archive, Moscow, fond 846: 1793, 1794 and 1798 by army cartographers, with Fiodor Chomentovski authoring 1793 and 1798 (the most accurate); the 1799 plan is by surveyor Michail Markovich. They mark ruined buildings in blue (L. Glemža 2007, pp. 383–391, hdl.handle.net/20.500.12259/38283). One record reads f. 846, inv. 2(?), item 368 for 1798 (unverified). The 1808 plan: the digital copy from the former Architecture Museum is at the Lithuanian Institute of History; Drėma attributes it to 'Karolis Grunertas' (unverified). A 1805 plan extract is at the Vilnius regional archive (F 9-36). Catalogue: 'Vilniaus miesto planai' (Lithuanian National Museum, 2016; 153 plans; ISBN 978-609-8039-96-2).

findings.claim: Georeferenced historical data exists: VilniausDNR reconstructs the 1808 map, and the Lithuanian Institute of History has a GIS of property plots
findings.detail: VilniausDNR (ID Vilnius with the Wróblewski Library of the Academy of Sciences; released for Vilnius's 700th anniversary in 2023) presents reconstructed topographies for 1808, 1845, 1911, 1938 and 1977 with a 'time travel' comparison, plus 50 medium-scale maps and old photographs and postcards. The Lithuanian Institute of History property GIS maps plot outlines on the 1808 plan, with 69 time slices from 1636 to 1790 built from tax lists; it rests on the 'Vilniaus archeologijos atlasas' (2006 CD). Use: the 1808 layer is the closest surveyed geometry to 1794 for the street grid and plots. It is after the 1799–1804 demolitions, so use the 1793/1798 Russian plans for the Lower Castle, walls and gates. Licensing and download terms were not found.

findings.claim: Later sources for back-dating: Wilczyński's Album Wileńskie (1845–75, public domain), Czechowicz's photographs (c.1865–1880s), Oziębłowski lithographs (1830s), Bułhak photographs (1910s)
findings.detail: Album Wileńskie: published by Jan Kazimierz Wilczyński (1806–1885), printed in Paris by Lemercier/Drouart; 353 sheets and 364 lithographs over 40 years; public domain; digitised on Polona and on Wikimedia Commons (Category:Album_Wileńskie, including a 138-page PDF). Józef Czechowicz (1818–1888) settled in Vilnius around 1865 and made about 200 outdoor views plus church interiors; albums c.1870 and small-format albums from about 1879. The largest collection is at the Lithuanian National Museum; Vilnius University Library holds 73; the National Museum in Warsaw also has some; Polona has an item '[Kościół katedralny]' dated 1879–1882. Public domain (author died 1888). Józef Oziębłowski lithographs of the 1830s (Lithuanian Art Museum) include the Castle Gate and Tribunal (1835) and Town Hall Square. Marceli Januszkiewicz's 1840 watercolour of the castles in the late 18th century is anachronistic. Jan Bułhak photographs of 1912–14 (Lithuanian Art Museum) cover the Pilies courtyards and Chapter houses; he died in 1950, so they are likely public domain in the EU. The Lithuanian National Art Museum's 'Vilniaus gatvės' pages give per-address histories for Pilies and Didžioji streets (www.lndm.lt/en/pilies-street/N-pilies-street/).

risks: 'Today's building, back-dated' fails at the head of the spine. Cathedral Square did not exist in 1794: the Castle Gate, the Tribunal, the old Bishops' house, the chapter and vicars' houses and the Lower Castle walls stood there, and the ground was about 1.5 m lower. The wall and all its gates also stood. Those zones need geometry from the 1793/1798 Russian plans, the 1787 'French' castle plan and the Fürstenhoff-collection plan, not from modern map data.

Some present buildings date from after 1794 and have no 1794 shape to back-date to. Examples: Aušros Vartų 5 (Philharmonic 1899–1902; the merchants' house in 1794), the Presidential Palace (1824–34), St Nicholas and St Paraskeva (1865), the Chodkiewicz palace frontage (1825–34) and the WWII-era gap at Konstantino Sirvydo skveras. These need reconstruction from the 1808 plan plus conjecture, and must be flagged in the art bible.

Sources conflict on key dates: Cathedral roof statues (1792 per VLE vs after 1799 per Drėma, Smuglewicz 1797 and Peszka 1808); the Gates of Dawn gallery (1789–99 vs 1830–40); the icon's date and revetment (c.1620–30 with 1670–1730s revetment vs 1520–30 with late-18th-century revetment); street lighting (18th-century oil lamps vs early 1800s); St Casimir's Orthodox conversion (1832/1836–40 vs 1841). Pick one reading and record it, rather than silently choosing.

In 1794 the Cathedral (work halted 1792) and the Town Hall (work halted 1793–97) were unfinished building sites. Modelling them as finished neoclassical landmarks would be anachronistic. Their exact 1794 state (portico, roof, scaffolding) is not documented in the sources found.

Many findings rest on popular-history and institutional web pages (ldkistorija.lt, neakivaizdinisvilnius.lt, Wikipedia, lndm.lt exhibition texts, tourist sites) rather than peer-reviewed monographs. Population figures in particular are unreliable.

Access and licensing: the 1793–99 plans are in the Russian military archive in Moscow (fond 846), which is hard to access remotely. No shelfmark was found for the Fürstenhoff-collection plan in Berlin. The National Museum in Kraków holds the Smuglewicz originals and claims copyright on its photographs. Licensing for the VilniausDNR data is unknown.

With remote reference only, per-building storey counts, window types and colours in 1794 cannot be confirmed for most houses. Generic rules (2–3 storeys, 45° tile roofs, no balconies or shopfronts) will be wrong for some buildings.

Setting spine-facing Jewish shops or residences would contradict the 1742 privilege, which excluded Jews from the Gates of Dawn–Cathedral route. The Jewish quarter should read as adjacent side streets (Žydų, Stiklių, Mėsinių, Gaono).
open_questions: How complete was the Cathedral exterior in April 1794: portico columns, Righi's pediment relief and Evangelists, roof, scaffolding? Are there any drawings from 1792–96 besides the 1797 Smuglewicz sketch at the National Museum in Kraków?
What state was the Town Hall in during 1794: which old walls stood, was there a roof, was the portico built? Did the Kossakowski gallows stand in front of a construction site?
Was the Gates of Dawn pilgrim gallery and staircase (Pietro de Rossi, designed c.1789) built by 1794, and in what form (open wooden balustrades?)
What exactly did the baroque top of the Cathedral bell tower look like before Šulcas's reconstruction? The only known depiction is a distant Smuglewicz panorama.

Were there any public oil street lanterns on Pilies or Didžioji in 1794? This needs primary magistrate records from the Lithuanian State Historical Archives (LVIA) or the full Gotalskis & Klimka 2006 text.

Per-building 1794 data (storeys, roof, façade, colour) for Pilies, Didžioji and Aušros Vartų: can the heritage register entries (kvr.kpd.lt), the 1808 plan and 19th-century property inventories be mined systematically?

What stood in 1794 on sites now occupied by post-1794 or post-war structures: Aušros Vartų 5, Konstantino Sirvydo skveras on Pilies, the buildings demolished in 1865 around St Nicholas, and those between the Chodkiewicz palace and its neighbour before 1825–34?
Who authored the 1808 plan (Grunert?), where is the original held, and can the VilniausDNR 1808 vector layer be downloaded and licensed?
What are the shelfmarks and reproduction rights for the Fürstenhoff-collection plan (Berlin State Library), the 1787 'French' castle plan (Kraków) and the fond 846 plans in Moscow?
What was St Casimir's used for in 1794, after the Jesuit suppression in 1773 and before it became a parish church in 1799? What did St Anne's bell tower look like before it was demolished in 1870?
Exactly how far did the 1737, 1748 and 1749 fires reach along the spine, street by street? Which Pilies and Didžioji houses escaped?
What were ordinary burgher houses painted in the 1790s? Is there any polychromy research on residential façades on Pilies or Didžioji?

checks.claim: The three great fires (2 June 1737, 11 June 1748, 8 June 1749) are the events that shaped the 1794 spine. The 1760 fire is mentioned only as 'a separate fire' that burned St Theresa's.
checks.correction: The three dates are right (ldkistorija; lt.wikipedia articles on the 1748 and 1749 fires). The report leaves out the fire of 28 May 1760. It started around 11 a.m. 'in one of the manors beyond the Gates of Dawn' and destroyed 557 properties, more than 1748 (469) or 1749 (292). Source: B. Manyś, '1760 metų gaisro Vilniuje pasekmės, remiantis Kurier Litewski pranešimais', Lietuvos istorijos metraštis 2017/2 (publ. 2018), pp. 167–179, based on Kurier Litewski nos. 7 (30 May 1760) and 8 (6 June 1760). That makes it the biggest fire of the century by count, and it hit the Aušros Vartų end of the spine directly. Façades there (St Theresa's, the Basilian Gate of 1761, the Holy Spirit area) were about 30 years old in 1794, not 45. Minor conflict: the official presidency site dates the Bishops' Palace fire to 14 June 1748, not 11 June.

checks.claim: Cathedral in 1794: Gucevičius's rebuild (from 1783) halted in 1792, resumed spring 1798 under Šulcas and finished 1801. The three roof statues were not yet in place.
checks.correction: Halt, resumption and completion are confirmed: work was cancelled in 1792 over Massalski's financial crisis, restarted in spring 1798 under Šulcas and finished in 1801 (ldkistorija; VLE gives 1783–1801). On the statues, VLE dates them to '1792, skulptorius K. Jelskis', but Kazimierz Jelski was born on 4 March 1782 (en.wikipedia). A 1792 date for him is effectively impossible. That strengthens the post-1798 reading (the 1797 Smuglewicz sketch, the 1799 wooden figures, the 1808 Peszka drawing), though the ekspertai.eu piece making that case is an opinion article. Two further corrections. (a) The side-façade statues are the 7 princes (1754) and 5 Jesuit saints (1754–68) carved for St Casimir's altars; they moved to the Cathedral only after St Casimir's was taken from Catholics in 1832 (katedra.lt). In 1794 they stood inside St Casimir's. (b) The 1769 storm is dated 2 September by ldkistorija and 2 November by other sources, not 2 November alone. The state of the portico and roof in April 1794 remains undocumented.

checks.claim: Cathedral bell tower: only the iron cross on the gilded drum dates from 1893. The classicist top stage, dials and obelisk are Šulcas's post-1798 work.
checks.correction: The Cathedral's own site says the third tier was rebuilt 'at the end of the 18th and beginning of the 19th century' and that '1893 m. suformuotas varpinės stogas': the roof itself was shaped in 1893, together with the cross on the gilded drum. So back-dating must replace the whole present roof and spire profile, not just the cross. Height today is 52 m, or 57 m with the cross. What the pre-Šulcas baroque top looked like remains unknown.

checks.claim: Lower Castle area: the Castle Gate was rebuilt in 1785 as a three-storey Tribunal building and demolished in 1837 (Tribunal 1836–37). The Palace of the Grand Dukes was demolished 1799–1801.
checks.correction: Castle Gate: rebuilt 1785 as a three-storey building for the Supreme Tribunal, demolished in 1837 for the Vilnius fortress, together with the neighbouring Tribunal building (lt.wikipedia 'Žemutinė pilis', via search summary; tartle.lt). Palace: demolished 1799–1801 on the order of Governor Ivan Frizel (1799), who contracted the Kremenchuk merchant Moisei Slutsky to pull it down. Abraham Schlossberg's two-storey house was built on the east-wing remains. The '1.5 m lower' ground figure comes from a single 20 × 20 m trench at the Gediminas monument site, just beyond St Casimir's chapel. Treat it as local, not square-wide.

checks.claim: All ten city gates and the wall stood in 1794; demolition ran 1799–1804.
checks.correction: Paul I ordered the demolition on 10 September 1799, with most of it done 1799–1802. Rūdninkai Gate went in 1800. The Trakai Gate was badly damaged in the 1794 fighting and repaired in October 1794; demolition began in 1803, was halted, resumed in 1804 and completed then (lt.wikipedia, LRT/Klimka, via search summary). Minor: en.wikipedia says the wall had nine gates plus the artillery bastion; its list of ten names includes the Castle Gate.

checks.claim: Town Hall: the tower collapsed 19 June 1781; Gucevičius's rebuild ran 1785/88–1799 and was halted 1793–95; a 50,000-rouble loan came in 1797.
checks.correction: Confirmed: the collapse on 19 June 1781 (ldkistorija; work had begun 9 June 1781), and '1785–99, on the old foundations and cellars' (VLE; vilniausrotuse.lt). Other sources say actual construction began in 1788 and ended in 1799. The halt blamed on 1793–95 and the 1797 loan of 50,000 roubles appear only in weak sources (yrasalis.lt, school essays), not in VLE or lndm. The building's state in April 1794 (walls, roof, portico) is undocumented.

checks.claim: 1794 timeline: the Act of Uprising was proclaimed on Town Hall Square on 24 April; Kossakowski was hanged there on 25 April; the Russian garrison was about 2,000 against fewer than 400; the assault came on 19–20 July; the city capitulated 11–12 August to Knorring's roughly 12,000; Gucevičius commanded the 1,500–2,000-strong city guard.
checks.correction: Details: the attack began on the night of 22/23 April at about 00:30. The garrison was about 2,000 men with 19 guns under Gen. Nikolai Arsenyev. The Act was read on the Town Hall Square on 24 April. Knorring attacked on 19 July with about 8,000 men against 500 regulars and 1,500 militia. He attacked again on 11 August with 12,000, and the city capitulated on 12 August under Gen. Antoni Chlewiński (en.wikipedia, pl.wikipedia). Gucevičius commanded the city guard only until he was wounded on 26 June (vilniausrotuse.lt), so he did not lead the July–August defence. The 'yellow dressing gown' and St Casimir's bells are unverified.

checks.claim: Presidential Palace (the old Bishops' Palace) was rebuilt 1824–34 by Stasov.
checks.correction: The official presidency site gives 1824–1832 (Stasov's design, carried out by Karol Podczaszyński). In 1794 it was still the residence of Bishop Ignacy Massalski, and Gucevičius had done some reconstruction work for him there. The report does not mention that Massalski was hanged by a mob in Warsaw on 28 June 1794. He was the patron of the Cathedral rebuild and a major real figure for the story.

checks.claim: St Anne's: its old bell tower, of unknown form, was demolished in 1870 and replaced by N. Chagin's neo-Gothic tower (1872/73). Otherwise the church appears as today.
checks.correction: The 1870 demolition and the 1872/73 Chagin tower are confirmed. But the demolished belfry was not of unknown date. lt.wikipedia: '1794 m. rekonstruota, nutinkuota, šalia pastatyta varpinė (architektas Mykolas Angelas Šulcas)', meaning in 1794 the church was reconstructed and plastered and a belfry by Šulcas was built beside it. Another source dates that belfry to 1802, and VLE lists 'rekonstruota 1794'. So in 1794 St Anne's was probably a work site, possibly plastered over its brick, and its belfry either under construction or not yet built.

checks.claim: St Paraskeva (Didžioji 2) in 1794 was a stocky, working church of Romanesque proportions, rebuilt only by Chagin in 1865.
checks.correction: lt.wikipedia: '1748 m. bažnyčia beveik visiškai sudegė', after which it 'stovėjo ilgus metus neremontuota ir be stogo' (it nearly burned out in 1748 and stood for many years unrepaired and roofless); it passed to the Uniates in 1795. en.wikipedia: destroyed by fire in 1748 and rebuilt in 1795. In 1794 it was most likely a roofless ruin or under repair. It was hemmed in by houses on three sides, with the fish market nearby (lndm), and there was no open square. Chagin's rebuild is dated 1864 by the wikis and 1865 by lndm.

checks.claim: St Casimir's had its baroque crown cupola by 1755 (Żebrowski); it became a parish church only from 1799, and its use in 1794 is unknown.
checks.correction: The cupola is confirmed: rebuilt after the 1749 fire by T. Žebrauskas (Żebrowski), 1749/50–1755, and the crown restored in 1942 (VLE). VLE says that after the Jesuit order was dissolved in 1773 the church served as a parish church. That gives a 1794 use and conflicts with the report's '1799' (from lndm). VLE gives 1841 for the handover to the Orthodox. In 1794 the church also still held the 12 altar statues that now stand on the Cathedral's side façades.

checks.claim: Gates of Dawn in 1794: the brick chapel stood without its 1829 classicist façade; the pilgrim gallery (Pietro de Rossi, c.1789) was built 1789–99, or alternatively 1830–40.
checks.correction: The 1829 late-classicist rebuild is confirmed by the shrine's official site. The wooden chapel of 1669–71 and the fire of 27 April 1715 are confirmed by lt.wikipedia. The gallery conflict stands: bernardinai.lt says it was built 1789–1799 to de Rossi's design, while lt.wikipedia says de Rossi designed it c.1789 but the 'spacious gallery' was built 1830–40. The Latin inscriptions on the present façade are not the original wording (ausrosvartai.lt describes swaps after 1863 and in 1933), which is irrelevant for 1794 since the façade is later anyway.

checks.claim: Plans: no shelfmark was found for the Fürstenhoff-collection plan in Berlin. The Russian 1793–99 plans are in RGVIA fond 846, possibly 'inv. 2(?), item 368' for 1798. Chomentovski drew the 1793 and 1798 plans.
checks.correction: A heritage-research annex published by Vilnius municipality cites: Chomentovski's 1798 plan at RGVIA (RVKIA) f. 846, op. 16, d. 21813, and Markovich's 1799 plan at f. 846, op. 16, d. 21815 (the second from a search summary). It says Chomentovski also drew a 1794 plan of the city and suburbs, and it gives the Fürstenhoff plan as 'PVBB [Staatsbibliothek zu Berlin], Kartografijos rinkinys, X 50203'. The same annex cites a 1790 plan by 'von Orlich' (PVBB Kart. Q19082; LNM AFP 4257) that the report missed. None of these has been checked against the SBB or RGVIA catalogues, so treat them as leads.

checks.claim: Public street lanterns in 1794 are 'doubtful at best'; oil lamps are documented from 1824 and gas from 1864.
checks.correction: Gas lamps are confirmed: 307 lit on 22 October 1864 (neakivaizdinisvilnius.lt, from archive records). But the one journal source, Gotalskis & Klimka, 'Vilniaus gatvių apšvietimas...', Mokslo ir technikos raida Lietuvoje 10 (2006), pp. 304–313, says in its abstract that 18th-century hemp-oil street lanterns burned seven months a year (15 Sep – 15 Apr) under dedicated keepers. The archive article says the main streets got their first lanterns only in the early 19th century. So the better source leans toward some public oil lamps existing before 1794, and 'doubtful at best' overstates the case. The Vilnius magistrate records (LVIA f. 458) would settle it.
